title: [FEATURE] Interactive selection of installed plugins for removal
body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

Managing plugins currently requires browsing a static table, copying or typing a package identifier, and running a separate command. Removal is particularly awkward when installed identities include a host, repository, and package subpath. Users should be able to select installed plugins by their recognizable names without reconstructing those identifiers.

#2749 already proposes interactive package selection for installation/search. This request covers the complementary removal workflow so adding and removing plugins can share a consistent interaction.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

Provide an opt-in interactive removal picker, for example `apm uninstall --interactive` and `apm uninstall --interactive --global` (exact command shape subject to maintainer preference).

- List installed plugins in the selected project or user scope, showing their name, source, and scope.
- Support filtering and selecting one or more plugins.
- Resolve selections directly to their installed dependency identities, including marketplace packages, rather than asking users to type aliases or full paths.
- Show the removal plan and ask for confirmation before applying it through the existing uninstall implementation. Cancellation must leave the installation unchanged.
- Keep scripted/non-interactive commands available; do not hang waiting for input in CI or without a suitable terminal.

Align the picker with the installation UX proposed in #2749. Reuse existing dependency ownership and removal rules rather than adding a separate cleanup mechanism.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

Use `apm deps list`, then copy the installed dependency into `apm uninstall`. This works as a command-line workflow, but long identifiers and truncated terminal tables make it inconvenient. A shell wrapper with an external picker would duplicate scope and identity handling outside APM.

**Additional context**

Requested after exercising marketplace registration, global installation, updates, and removal with APM 0.30.0. The goal is a small, consistent interactive workflow for adding and removing plugins, not a full-screen package-management application.

Related installation proposal: #2749.

title: Separate automated triage recommendations from human approval
body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
Phase 1 defines human contribution/governance authority, but the triage skill and workflow can still imply implementation approval, assign milestones, and conflate deferred work with accepted work. The automated write permissions must match the human policy rather than relying on prompt wording alone.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Phase 2 of the approved governance/roadmap stack, based on #2954 (corrected head 43391a54c8; full Deploy Docs CI passed). @danielmeppiel explicitly approved this phase in the interactive planning session on 2026-09-11 after the docs regression was fixed.

Approved scope:
- Make the triage package recommend a decision and a short proposed scope/acceptance brief. Remove agent ratification, silence-as-approval, and defer-later-to-accepted semantics.
- Restrict workflow write operations to permitted classification and advisory-processing metadata. No automated human acceptance, contributor invitations, or release-milestone assignments. Preserve human edits.
- Define a canonical label contract separating human decision states (needs-triage, needs-design, accepted, deferred) from bot-processing metadata. Keep useful type/area labels without a mandatory five-axis taxonomy for contributors.
- Prepare legacy-label migration rules and update directly affected consumers and regression tests. Do not apply the live migration in this phase.
- Preserve the human maintainer roster and approval rules approved in Phase 1. Labels alone are not authorization; enforcement of the human approval record belongs to a later phase.

Acceptance criteria:
- Automated recommendations cannot authorize implementation or make release commitments through the workflow's allowed operations.
- Deferred work is never emitted/applied as accepted.
- Human decision state and bot deduplication/processing state are distinct, with an explicit safe rollout/legacy-compatibility approach.
- Direct consumers and generated workflow/skill artifacts remain coherent; relevant tests and validation cover the new boundary.
- No changes to runtime product behavior, GitHub role grants, the live roadmap, existing labels/issues/PRs, or backlog cleanup.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
Keeping consequential write tools and only telling the agent not to use them leaves a weak boundary. Treating any acceptance label as proof of human approval is not safe because GitHub has no per-label role ACL. Replacing the existing process with more agent panels would add overhead without repairing decision authority.

**Additional context**
Depends on the policy in #2953 / #2954. This PR must be stacked on #2954, not independently based on main. Its body should be concise and custom, not follow the PR-description skill format. Roadmap management, eligibility checks, and full retrospective cleanup remain later phases with separate approval; cleanup is last.

title: [BUG] Git-subpath dependency `content_hash` records CRLF bytes on Windows when the system gitconfig sets `core.autocrlf=true`; lockfile is not portable to Linux
body:
**Describe the bug**

On a Windows host whose *system* gitconfig sets `core.autocrlf=true` (the Git for Windows installer default), `apm install` / `apm lock` materialize git-subpath dependencies (`owner/repo/<subdir>#<ref>`) with CRLF line endings. `compute_package_hash()` hashes raw bytes by design (see the docstring in `src/apm_cli/utils/content_hash.py`), so every package `content_hash` written to `apm.lock.yaml` is a CRLF-byte hash. The same commit materialized on Linux hashes differently, so:

- a lockfile generated on the Windows host fails `apm install --frozen` on a Linux runner with a content-hash mismatch, and
- a lockfile generated on Linux fails `apm install --frozen` on the Windows host.

This is the same failure class as #2187 and #2619, but the CRLF bytes here come from **git's own checkout of upstream content**, not from a synthetic file APM writes, so neither of those fixes covers it. `bare_cache.materialize_from_bare()` does run `git config core.autocrlf false` on the consumer clone before `git checkout` (src/apm_cli/deps/bare_cache.py, "CRLF determinism" block), but the materialized tree on this host still contains CRLF.

It is not a stale-cache artifact: with `APM_CACHE_DIR` pointed at a fresh empty directory the checkout is still CRLF.

**To Reproduce**

On Windows where `git config --system core.autocrlf` prints `true` and no user or repo config overrides it:

1. Create a manifest with one git-subpath dependency on any public repository whose text files are committed with LF, for example a skills directory:
   ```yaml
   dependencies:
     apm:
       - owner/repo/skills/<skill-name>#<tag>
   ```
2. Point apm at an empty cache and lock: `set APM_CACHE_DIR=%TEMP%\apm-cache-fresh` then `apm lock`.
3. Note the `content_hash` recorded for the dependency.
4. Lock the same manifest on Linux (or on the same Windows host with git's env-only override, see workaround). The `content_hash` differs.
5. `apm install --frozen` with the Windows lock on Linux reports a content-hash mismatch for the dependency.

I confirmed the cause by running apm's own `compute_package_hash()` over both materializations of the same commit: the CRLF tree reproduces the value in the Windows-generated lock, the LF tree reproduces the value the Linux runner computes. Checking the materialized checkout under `APM_CACHE_DIR` for `\r` bytes shows they are present on the Windows host and absent under the workaround.

**Expected behavior**

A git-subpath dependency at a pinned commit should hash identically on every OS regardless of the host's `core.autocrlf` setting. That is the invariant the `content_hash.py` docstring already states ("git-materialized content already does (identical bytes at a pinned commit on every OS)"). The per-clone `core.autocrlf=false` that `materialize_from_bare` sets should be sufficient. On this host it is not.

**Environment (please complete the following information):**

 - OS: Windows 11 (10.0.26300)
 - Python Version: 3.12.10
 - APM Version: 0.30.0 (a lock this host produced on an earlier 0.2x release shows the same class of mismatch, so it is not new in 0.30)
 - VSCode Version (if relevant): N/A
 - Git: 2.54.0.windows.1, system gitconfig `core.autocrlf=true`, no user or repo override
 - Linux side (for comparison): `apm-cli==0.30.0` on ubuntu-latest and in `python:3.12-slim`

**Logs**

`apm install --frozen` on Linux against the Windows-generated lock reports a content-hash mismatch per git-subpath package (expected = the CRLF hash in the lock, got = the LF hash). I can attach the exact output if useful.

**Additional context**

Workaround that fixes it completely: run apm with git's environment-only config override and a dedicated cache directory, so checkouts that were already materialized with CRLF are never reused:

```
GIT_CONFIG_COUNT=1
GIT_CONFIG_KEY_0=core.autocrlf
GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_0=false
APM_CACHE_DIR=<fresh dir>
```

With that in apm's environment the same `apm lock` records the LF hashes and the lockfile passes `apm install --frozen` on Linux. Setting `core.autocrlf=false` in `~/.gitconfig` also works. Both are host-side mitigations. The point of this issue is that a default Git for Windows install produces non-portable lockfiles out of the box, and nothing in apm's output says so.

UNVERIFIED hypothesis on the mechanism, for whoever picks this up: an env-level override fixes it while the per-repo `git config` in `materialize_from_bare` does not, which suggests some git invocation that writes working-tree bytes for these dependencies is not running against that consumer clone's config. Candidates: a different materialization path for subpath deps than `materialize_from_bare` (e.g. `GitCache._create_checkout`), or a copy step from the checkout into `apm_modules/` that goes through text mode. I have not traced it.

Related: #2187, #2619, #1952, and `scripts/crlf_invariance_probe.py`, which covers per-file hashing and APM-written synthetic files but not a real `core.autocrlf=true` git checkout of a subpath dependency through the package-hash path.

title: [BUG] apm install fails on Windows: shutil.which(str(directory / name)) never resolves git.exe (PATHEXT not applied)
body:
## What happened

`apm install`/`apm update` fails on Windows with:

```
Failed to download dependency <owner>/<repo>: Failed to clone repository: git executable not found on PATH. Please install git: https://git-scm.com/downloads
```

...even when `git` is installed and resolvable on `PATH` (verified with `git --version` / `(Get-Command git).Source` in the same shell, in both Git Bash and native PowerShell).

## Root cause

`apm_cli/utils/git_env.py`, in `_resolve_trusted_executable()`:

```python
candidate = shutil.which(str(directory / name))
```

On Windows, `shutil.which()` only appends `PATHEXT` extensions (`.EXE`, `.CMD`, …) when the given command has **no directory component**. Once you join a directory onto the name (`str(directory / name)`), `shutil.which` takes the "already a path" branch and checks the literal string for an exact, executable match — it never tries `git.exe`, `git.EXE`, etc. Since the file on disk is `git.exe` and never a bare `git`, the check always fails, for every directory on `PATH`, regardless of whether Git is installed.

Minimal repro (no APM involved):

```python
import shutil
from pathlib import Path

d = Path(r"C:\Program Files\Git\cmd")
shutil.which(str(d / "git"))        # -> None  (this is the current code's call shape)
shutil.which("git", path=str(d))    # -> 'C:\Program Files\Git\cmd\git.EXE'  (correct)
```

Same failure mode affects `get_gh_executable()` (`gh` resolution) for the same reason.

## Fix

Pass the command name and directory separately so `shutil.which`'s Windows `PATHEXT` handling actually runs:

```python
# apm_cli/utils/git_env.py, _resolve_trusted_executable()
- candidate = shutil.which(str(directory / name))
+ candidate = shutil.which(name, path=str(directory))
```

Verified this one-line change resolves `git`/`gh` correctly via the existing per-directory loop, with the existing trusted-directory exclusion logic (`_executable_exclusion_root`) untouched.

## Environment

- `apm-cli` 0.30.0 (`pip install apm-cli`)
- Windows 11, git 2.43.0.windows.1 (`C:\Program Files\Git\cmd\git.exe`), gh CLI installed
- Reproduced identically in Git Bash and native `powershell.exe`

title: [cli-consistency] CLI Consistency Report - 2026-09-14
body:
## CLI Consistency Report

**Date**: 2026-09-14
**APM Version**: Agent Package Manager (APM) CLI version 0.30.0 (6f3dd39)
**Commands Inspected**: 23 (`apm --help` + init, install, uninstall, update, compile, run, deps, deps list/tree/info/clean/update, mcp, mcp search/show/install, config, config set/get/list, runtime, runtime setup) plus targeted checks of `apm audit`, `apm lock`, `apm lock export`, and error-path commands.

### Summary

| Severity | Count |
|----------|-------|
| High | 0 |
| Medium | 0 |
| Low | 3 |

No high or medium severity issues were found. The CLI help text is accurate, matches the documentation in `docs/src/content/docs/reference/cli/` and `README.md`, and error handling is clean (proper exit code 2 with usage messages, no stack traces) for invalid flags and missing required arguments.

---

### Low Severity

#### 1. `apm init --target` is missing the `-t` short flag used elsewhere

- **Command**: `apm init --help` vs `apm install --help` / `apm update --help` / `apm compile --help` / `apm deps update --help`
- **Problem**: Every other command that accepts a target list exposes both `-t` and `--target`, but `apm init` only accepts the long form `--target`.
- **Evidence**:
  ```
  # apm init --help
  --target TARGET            Comma-separated target list (skip prompt, write directly)

  # apm install --help
  -t, --target TARGET             Target harness(es) to deploy to. ...

  # apm update --help
  -t, --target TARGET           Agent target(s) to update for. ...

  # apm compile --help
  -t, --target TARGET             Target platform (comma-separated). ...

  # apm deps update --help
  -t, --target TARGET           Target platform (comma-separated). ...
  ```
- **Suggested Fix**: Add the `-t` short alias to `apm init --target` for consistency with `install`, `update`, `compile`, and `deps update`, or document why `init` intentionally omits it.

#### 2. `apm init --format` is missing the `-f` short flag used by other format options

- **Command**: `apm init --help` vs `apm audit --help` / `apm lock export --help`
- **Problem**: `apm audit` and `apm lock export` both expose `-f, --format`, but `apm init --format` (discovery report format) only accepts the long form.
- **Evidence**:
  ```
  # apm init --help
  --format [text|json|yaml]  Discovery report format  [default: text]

  # apm audit --help
  -f, --format [text|json|sarif|markdown]  Output format: text (default), json, sarif ...

  # apm lock export --help
  -f, --format [cyclonedx|spdx]  SBOM output format  [default: cyclonedx]
  ```
- **Suggested Fix**: Add `-f` as a short alias for `apm init --format`, matching the pattern used by `audit` and `lock export`.

title: Clarify package-relative links and committed target-owned directories
body:
I’m exploring APM and trying to understand the intended workflow around target-owned deployment directories (such as .github) and package-relative links.

The documentation recommends committing target-owned directories such as .github so that contributors have access to the deployed manifests/context immediately after cloning the repository, before running apm install.

However, I’m having difficulty understanding how this works when the manifests in .github contain package-relative links.

According to the [Package Relative Links](https://microsoft.github.io/apm/producer/package-relative-links/) documentation, these links are resolved to files under apm_modules/.

Since apm_modules/ is generated/populated when apm install is run and is normally not committed, this appears to create the following situation:

After git clone:

my-project/
├── apm.yml
├── apm.lock.yaml
├── .github/
│   └── agents/
│       └── example.agent.md   ✅ committed
└── apm_modules/               ❌ not present

If example.agent.md contains a package-relative link such as:

../../apm_modules/<package>/references/example.md

then the manifest itself is available immediately after cloning, but the referenced content is not.

After running:

apm install

the situation becomes:

my-project/
├── .github/
│   └── agents/
│       └── example.agent.md   ✅
└── apm_modules/
    └── <package>/
        └── references/
            └── example.md      ✅
Main question

If .github manifests can contain package-relative links that cannot be resolved until apm install has been run, what is the practical benefit of committing those manifests to the repository?

In other words, is the intended workflow:

git clone
   ↓
.github manifests are immediately available
   ↓
but some links may not work
   ↓
apm install
   ↓
apm_modules becomes available
   ↓
links now resolve

If so, is the main purpose of committing .github to provide the agent manifests themselves immediately after cloning, while accepting that references to package-owned content will not work until installation?

Or is there a recommended approach for structuring packages/manifests so that the committed .github content remains fully functional before apm install?

Questions

I’d particularly appreciate clarification on:

What is the intended purpose of committing .github manifests if their package-relative links may not resolve after a fresh clone?

Should contributors be expected to run apm install before the .github manifests can be considered fully functional?

Are package-relative links inside committed .github manifests expected to be temporarily broken after cloning?
Is there a recommended pattern for avoiding this situation—for example, keeping certain content directly in .github rather than linking to package-owned files?

Is the distinction between "manifest available after clone" and "manifest fully functional after apm install" something that could be made more explicit in the documentation?

The main thing I’m trying to understand is whether this behavior is an intentional design trade-off, and what users are expected to gain by committing the .github manifests when those manifests may depend on content that does not exist until apm install is executed.

Thanks!

title: [BUG] Cursor user-scope install skips instructions (no ~/.cursor/rules/*.mdc)
body:
**Describe the bug**

`apm install -g` / `apm update -g` for the Cursor target silently skips the `instructions` primitive. Agents, skills, and hooks are written under `~/.cursor/`, but **zero** instruction files are deployed.

This is not an error: `KNOWN_TARGETS["cursor"]` currently sets `user_supported="partial"` and `unsupported_user_primitives=("instructions",)`, so `for_scope(user_scope=True)` drops instructions before any integrator runs.

Cursor already has a file-backed rules surface (`.cursor/rules/*.mdc` via the existing `cursor_rules` transform). Project-scope installs use that path; user-scope installs do not, because of the exclusion above. Docs that treat Cursor global rules as Settings-UI-only contradict Cursor’s documented `.mdc` rules layout.

**To Reproduce**

1. Use a package that ships `.apm/instructions/` (or any APM package with instruction files).
2. Run `apm install -g --target cursor`.
3. Inspect `~/.cursor/rules/` (and the install output).
4. Observe that instruction `.mdc` files are not created, while other Cursor user-scope primitives from the same package are.

**Expected behavior**

- Cursor is fully user-scope supported.
- `apm install -g --target cursor` deploys instructions via the same `cursor_rules` transform as project scope, to `~/.cursor/rules/*.mdc`.
- `apm uninstall -g --target cursor <pkg>` removes those `.mdc` files.
- The user-scope unsupported warning no longer lists `cursor (instructions)`.
- Docs / CHANGELOG match runtime behavior.

**Proposed scope** (for maintainer agreement before implementation)

In scope:

1. Mark Cursor `user_supported=True` and clear `unsupported_user_primitives` so instructions survive `for_scope(user_scope=True)`.
2. Reuse the existing `cursor_rules` writer — no new format; user scope emits `.mdc` under `~/.cursor/rules/`.
3. Tests: scope profile, install/uninstall cycle for `.mdc` + agents, covering-array row `cursor-instruction-user`, warning text.
4. Docs: primitives-and-targets output-directory table and targets-matrix deploy-directory / user-scope notes should list `~/.cursor/` at user scope.

Out of scope:

- Automating Cursor Settings UI “User Rules” (plaintext is additive, not a missing APM primitive).
- Fixing Cursor cloud-agent workspaces that are not under `$HOME` (Cursor-side resolution; document as a caveat).

**Environment**

- OS: macOS / Linux / Windows (user-scope home-directory deploy)
- APM: current `main` (Cursor still `user_supported="partial"` with `unsupported_user_primitives=("instructions",)`)
- Target: Cursor

**Logs**

Silent omission: install succeeds with no instruction files and no error that instructions were skipped for Cursor at user scope (beyond the general partial-support warning).

**Additional context**

Implementation already exists on closed PR https://github.com/microsoft/apm/pull/2506 (closed in the issue-first intake reset because there was no tracking issue). Please agree scope here so that PR can be reopened and reused — no need to start over.

Related discussion on that PR: Cursor’s project rules are `.cursor/rules` `.mdc` files; user-scope file deploy to `~/.cursor/rules` is distinct from Settings UI User Rules. Cloud agents outside `$HOME` remain a documented Cursor-side gap.

title: [BUG]: UnicodeDecodeError: 'gbk' codec can't decode byte on Windows during 'apm install'
body:
Description
On Windows environments (PowerShell / Command Prompt), running apm install fails with a UnicodeDecodeError in the underlying subprocess reader thread when resolving dependencies. This happens because Python defaults to the system code page (gbk / CP936 on Simplified Chinese Windows) rather than UTF-8 when reading standard output/error from spawned child processes (e.g., git or sub-commands with UTF-8 characters).

Steps to Reproduce
Run PowerShell on a Windows system using standard Chinese locale (chcp 936).

Add dependencies containing UTF-8 characters (e.g., non-ASCII commit logs, quotes, or descriptions) in apm.yml.

Run:

PowerShell
apm install ; apm compile
Observe the exception during package resolution.

Expected Behavior
apm should handle process I/O using UTF-8 explicitly (e.g., setting encoding="utf-8", errors="replace" or errors="backslashreplace" in subprocess.Popen / stream readers), allowing dependency resolution to finish without crashing regardless of the OS system locale.

Actual Behavior / Stack Trace
Plaintext
PS D:\2-gerrit\Jenkins\jenkins-platform.worktrees\workflow> apm install ; apm compile
[>] Installing dependencies from apm.yml...
[>] Resolving lsp-infra-hub-jenkins-cli...
[>] Resolving awesome-copilot-multi-stage-dockerfile...
[>] Resolving lsp-infra-hub-apm-skill-creator...
Exception in thread Thread-64 (_readerthread):
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "threading.py", line 1075, in _bootstrap_inner
  File "threading.py", line 1012, in run
  File "subprocess.py", line 1599, in _readerthread
UnicodeDecodeError: 'gbk' codec can't decode byte 0x94 in position 711: illegal multibyte sequence
Environment
OS: Windows (Simplified Chinese, default codepage 936 / GBK)

Shell: PowerShell

Tool: APM (Agent Package Manager)

Python Version: 3.x

title: [perf-scan] 2026-09-25 -- performance opportunities found
body:
## Performance Scan - 2026-09-25

Automated scan of src/apm_cli/ for algorithmic performance anti-patterns.
1 finding identified.

### Findings

#### [F] Sequential independent I/O -- src/apm_cli/commands/install.py:295-484

- Current: O(n) sequential network round-trips -- `_resolve_package_references`
  iterates `packages` one at a time (line 295) and, for each package that
  isn't registry-routed or git-semver-eligible, calls
  `_validate_package_exists` (line 466) synchronously. That function
  performs a blocking GitHub/ADO REST API probe (`requests.get`, see
  `install/validation.py:693` and `:796`) or a shallow git fetch
  (`github_downloader_validation.py:770-806`) per package, with no data
  dependency between iterations (each package's accessibility check is
  independent of the others).
- Proposed: O(1) wall-clock round-trips (bounded by `max_workers`) using a
  `concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor`, the same pattern already applied
  in `commands/outdated.py:713-761` (`_check_parallel`/`_check_parallel_plain`)
  and `deps/apm_resolver.py:830` for analogous per-dependency network probes.
- Fix: Wrap the per-package accessibility probe (and its git-semver /
  registry-ref branches, which are cheap/local) in a bounded
  `ThreadPoolExecutor.map`/`as_completed` call inside
  `_resolve_package_references`, preserving per-package error handling
  (`GitUrlRewriteError`/`GitUrlRewriteProbeError`) and outcome ordering, so
  `apm install pkg1 pkg2 pkg3 ...` validates all packages concurrently
  instead of one network round-trip at a time.

### Scan coverage

- src/apm_cli/ (485 files scanned)
- Patterns checked: A (quadratic loops), B (linear scan in loop),
  C (unconditional expensive ops), D (redundant config parsing),
  E (heavy top-level imports), F (sequential independent I/O)
